title: Chiefs v Reds: Five takeaways as Damian McKenzie masterclass overshadowed by 'sickening' injury to All Blacks star - Planet Rugby
content: Chiefs fly-half Damian McKenzie scored 26 points in the win over the Reds. Following the Chiefs’ 46-24 win over the Reds in Super Rugby Pacific, here are our five takeaways from the last of the three qualifying finals at FMG Stadium Waikato in Hamilton. Damian McKenzie made a 26-point return from concussion to book the Chiefs a home semi-final against Crusaders in a match overshadowed by a sickening head injury to All Blacks star Wallace Sititi. McKenzie scored two tries and landed seven of his eight kicks at goal as Waikato’s finest twice came from behind to beat a gutsy Queensland outfit in head coach Les Kiss’ final match in charge before taking over the Wallabies. But celebrations at booking a last-four clash with the Crusaders were dampened by the loss of Sititi, who was knocked out in the first quarter by an accidental blow to the head from a team-mate. Amid concerning scenes the game was stopped for 10 minutes as the number eight received extensive treatment before being taken away on the back of a buggy. The Chiefs fell behind after Sititi‘s departure but recovered their composure to lead at the break and then win the second half 24-7, adding to Kyren Taumoefolau’s first period brace with tries by Samisoni Taukei’aho, McKenzie (2) and Isaac Hutchinson. They take on the Crusaders in Hamilton next Friday knowing they will need to raise their level from the regular season when they were beaten home and away by the 13-time champions. Sititi will almost certainly miss the rest of the Super Rugby campaign and could be a doubt for the All Blacks’ opening Nations Championship clash with France on July 4 after a ‘friendly fire’ blow to the head that left him shaking on the ground. The 23-year-old back-row is a key man not only for the Chiefs but also for a national team about to be taken over by Dave Rennie. How much he means to his team-mates quickly became apparent at the final whistle. “I want to send our love and our prayers to Wally,” McKenzie interjected at the start of his player of the match on-field interview. “Hopefully he’s doing alright. We’re all behind you, brother.” Super Rugby Pacific semi-finals: Blues claim ‘lucky losers’ tag with fixtures, dates, kick-off times and how to watch confirmed Chiefs captain Luke Jacobson added: “Thoughts and prayers with Wallace. Never nice seeing your team mate like that. We know he’s in the best of hands, but thoughts and prayers to him and his family.” Lukhan Salakaia-Loto was initially held responsible for the incident, sent to the sin bin by referee James Doleman. He was booed by the crowd when returning to the field. But replays showed that while he made the initial tackle, the damage was done by a Chiefs team-mate following Sititi into the breakdown. McKenzie was back in action for the first time since being knocked out by a boot to the face playing against the Highlanders last month – and how thankful his team were for that. With the Reds leading on the stroke of half-time, the 31-year-old fly-half landed the conversion which sent his side into the break ahead and then took the game away from the visitors by scoring the game’s next two tries. A split-second lapse in concentration from the Aussies was punished ruthlessly by McKenzie, taking a quick tap and diving over, and the Invercargill-born points machine put the game to bed with his second on 66 minutes. In between those scores he teamed up with the outstanding Cortez Ratima to make a try-saving tackle on Reds replacement Treyvon Pritchard. He then put a cherry on the cake with a spectacular 20-metre pass out the back door which Hutchinson ran in from almost halfway to seal the win. No Australian side had won a play-off match in Aotearoa in 21 attempts dating back 30 years. The last time the Reds won a post-season game anywhere away from home was in 1995, the amateur days of Super 10. History was therefore stacked against Queensland on a wet and cold evening on New Zealand’s North Island. But what a decent fist they made of overcoming it. Crusaders v Blues: Five takeaways as ‘ruthless’ champions, inspired by All Blacks snubs, punish ‘truly terrible tackle’ to extend insane record When Salakaia-Loto gave them a shock lead with the game’s first try on six minutes, it did more than give the visitors hope; it brought back uncomfortable memories for Chiefs fans of last year’s quarter-final. On that occasion, having secured the minor premiership with only three defeats in the regular season, they were stunned by sixth-placed Blues, losing to a last-gasp Josh Beehre score. Those Waikato nerves were back on display as Auckland-born lock Salakaia-Loto dotted down after fine work by the ball-juggling Fraser McReight and ever-alert Tate McDermott. Even though the home side bounced back strongly with tries by Taumoefolau – brilliantly made by Ratima – and Taukei’aho, the Reds reclaimed the lead. Loosehead prop Aidan Ross, who played 101 times for Chiefs between 2017-25, crossed against his former team. The fact Reds were down to 14, with Salakaia-Loto in the sin bin, only added to the sense of achievement. Even when McKenzie put his side back in charge the Reds would not go quietly; Matt Faessler scoring for Carter Gordon to convert and reduce the arrears to a dozen points. It was still not enough, however, and the interminable wait for Australian rugby goes on. Defeat marked the end of Kiss’ three-year tenure in Queensland but Australia‘s new head coach steps into Joe Schmidt’s shoes with a bit more optimism after this. The Brumbies’ 66-point thrashing in Wellington on Friday was a demoralising loss for all of Aussie rugby and Queensland’s elimination means an all-Kiwi semi-final. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. But the spirit shown by the Reds, particularly in the first half, augurs well going forward. The fight from Fraser McReight, on his 100th cap, Harry Wilson and McDermott reminded us just how good this Wallaby trio is. Gordon, too, let nobody down. “We put up a great shift and went into half-time full of confidence,” said McReight. “But credit to them (Chiefs) they were able to execute a lot better than we were. “We did throw everything into it. The fight from our group all year has been outstanding. That’s all you can ask for. They definitely delivered that tonight. I am proud of the boys.” READ MORE: Chiefs v Reds: Result, stats and line-ups from the Super Rugby Pacific Qualifying Final The teams ahead of Super Rugby Pacific's play-off clashes for this weekend. title: Canon EOS R6 V vs C50: Worth $1,400 Less? - Fstoppers
content: The Canon EOS R6 V lands at $2,500 with active cooling, IBIS, open gate 7K, and internal Raw — a spec sheet that would have cost you significantly more just a couple of years ago. The obvious question is how it actually performs against cameras like the Sony FX3 at $4,300 and the Canon EOS C50 at $3,900, and whether the gap in price reflects a meaningful gap in real-world image quality. Coming to you from Josh Sattin, this detailed early review puts the Canon EOS R6 V through its paces alongside the C50, which shares the same sensor. Sattin shoots sample footage in 7K open gate using the XF-HEVC codec and tests 4K in both full frame and crop modes, including some wildlife footage using the Canon RF 100-500mm. The image quality comparison between the R6 V and the C50 is one of the more useful parts of the video. Sattin grades the R6 V footage and copies that grade directly to the C50, and the results are close enough that he says mixing the two as an A and B camera setup wouldn't be a problem. The window test for dynamic range tells a slightly different story, where the C50 holds a small but visible edge in the shadows, which Sattin attributes to a few specific factors worth understanding if you're deciding between the two. One of those factors is IBIS itself. Sattin explains that in-body image stabilization generates heat even when it's turned off, which can introduce more noise compared to a camera without it. So the C50, which lacks IBIS, has a thermal advantage in that regard. The fan in the R6 V offsets some of that by keeping the sensor cooler than the Canon EOS R6 Mark III can manage without one, which means the R6 V likely sits somewhere between the R6 Mark III and the C50 in dynamic range performance. Sattin also touches on rolling shutter numbers (13.2 milliseconds in oversampled 4K at both 24 and 60 fps, and 6.6 milliseconds in 4K 120) and runs through autofocus performance, stabilization samples at 15mm and 20mm, and a body cap noise test confirming an informal second base ISO at 6,400 that behaves much like the C50's stated dual native ISO. Sattin also spends real time on the new Canon RF 20-50mm f/4L IS PZ, which arrived as a surprise alongside the camera. At 20mm on the wide end with a power zoom switch built in, it's compact enough that Sattin says it may replace carrying both his Canon RF 15-35mm f/2.8L IS USM and Canon RF 24-70mm f/2.8L IS USM for travel and run-and-gun work. The f/4 maximum aperture is a real trade-off, but Sattin points out that at high ISO the R6 V handles itself well enough that it rarely becomes a practical limitation outdoors. The video also covers where the R6 V fits against the Nikon Z6R, the Panasonic Lumix S1 Mark II, and what C50 owners should realistically think about before considering a switch, along with Sattin's own honest take on whether he'd sell his C50 to get one. Check out the video above for the full rundown from Sattin. Alex Cooke is a Cleveland-based photographer and meteorologist. He teaches music and enjoys time with horses and his rescue dogs.

volume 10,  Article number: 60 (2026) Cite this article Two-dimensional MXenes have emerged as promising support materials for electrocatalysts due to their high electrical conductivity and tunable surface chemistry. This study introduces a hydrothermal synthesis approach using NH4F as an additive to fabricate CoFe@V2CTx composites with systematically varied vanadium content. The NH4F-mediated hydrothermal method redirected crystallization from large catalytically inert crystals toward interfacially nucleated CoFOH and FeOOH phases at the V2CTx surface, reaching maximum abundance in the catalytically optimal composition CFV17. CFV17 demonstrated a reduced overpotential of 304 mV at 10 mA cm−2, a reduction in charge transfer resistance, and the lowest Tafel slope in the series. Operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy at the Co and Fe K-edges confirmed that CFV17 achieved cobalt and iron oxidation states exceeding their Co3+ and Fe3+ references at 150 mV lower potential compared to pure CoFe, mechanistically justifying the enhanced OER activity. Post-stability ICP-OES analysis confirmed that V2CTx stabilizes the CoFe active phase against dissolution. This work establishes V–O–Fe interfacial coordination as the central mechanistic principle leading to OER enhancement in CoFe@V2CTx composites and demonstrates that the NH4F hydrothermal synthesis route enables the compositional and interfacial control required to maximize this effect. The transition to sustainable energy systems necessitates efficient methods for hydrogen production through water electrolysis. Anion exchange membrane (AEM) water electrolyzers offer advantages over proton exchange membrane (PEM) systems, including the ability to use non-precious metal catalysts and potentially lower costs. However, the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) at the anode in alkaline media remains a critical bottleneck due to its sluggish four-electron transfer kinetics, requiring the development of highly active and stable electrocatalysts1. Hence, developing and fundamentally understanding catalysts in alkaline media is a prerequisite to establishing next-generation materials for AEM electrolyzers. Transition metal-based catalysts, particularly those containing iron (Fe) and cobalt (Co), have shown promise as OER catalysts in alkaline media2,3,4,5,6. The Co:Fe molar ratio is a critical compositional parameter governing OER activity in CoFe-based systems. For example, Burke et al. demonstrated that the intrinsic activity of Co1-xFex(OOH) peaks at x≈0.6–0.7, approximately 100-fold above that of Fe-free CoOOH, while more recent studies on CoFe layered double hydroxides have confirmed a volcano-shaped dependence of OER performance on Fe content, with excess Fe becoming detrimental above an optimal loading4,7. Beyond metal ratio, anion engineering through fluoride incorporation has emerged as an additional strategy for enhancing CoFe catalyst performance: fluoride coexistence with metal–O bonds has been shown to modulate the electronic structure of cobalt and iron centers through ligand field effects, with Co(OH)F and CoFe fluoride compounds demonstrating competitive OER activity in alkaline media 8,9. However, CoFe-based materials often suffer from limited electrical conductivity and stability under operating conditions, motivating the exploration of conductive support materials10. MXenes, represented by the general formula Mn+1XnTx (where M is an early transition metal, X is carbon and/or nitrogen, and Tx represents surface terminations), have recently emerged as exceptional support materials for electrocatalysts. Their metallic conductivity, hydrophilic surfaces, and rich surface chemistry make them ideal platforms for catalyst immobilization 11,12,13,14,15,16. The combination of CoFe-based materials with MXene supports has since attracted substantial attention as a strategy to overcome the intrinsic conductivity limitations of transition metal LDHs. Hao et al. demonstrated that growing CoFe-LDH on Ti3C2Tx nanosheets not only improved charge transfer efficiency but also suppressed the restacking of LDH platelets, resulting in an overpotential of 319 mV at 10 mA cm−217. These findings underscored that intimate interfacial contact between the 2D MXene scaffold and the LDH phase is critical for catalytic enhancement, with physical mixing of the two components offering markedly inferior performance compared to in-situ grown heterostructures. More recently, in 2024, Sheng et al. developed a CoFe-LDH and Ti3C2Tx MXene composite material for OER catalysis exhibiting an overpotential of 301 mV at 10 mA cm−2, along with a Tafel slope of 43 mV dec−118. The authors explored the role of MXene terminations in influencing the charge transfer between the MXene and CoFe-LDH and showed both by theoretical and experimental methods that the O-terminations on the MXene surface significantly reduced the rate-limiting energy barriers. Ti3C2Tx has been widely adopted due to its ease of synthesis and established processing protocols, but its Fermi-level electronic structure is dominated by Ti 3d bands that are relatively inert toward the oxygen intermediates central to the OER mechanism19. Additionally, Ti3C2Tx under OER conditions can oxidize to TiO2, which is passivating. In contrast, vanadium in V2CTx is multivalent, accessing oxidation states (II–V), and its d-orbital manifold generates a pronounced density of states (DOS) near the Fermi level. Theoretical investigations by Zhao et al. on single-atom Co anchored to different MXene substrates revealed that Co@V2CTx exhibited the lowest energy barrier in the rate-determining step of the OER among the series Co@Ti3C2Tx, Co@Nb2CTx, and Co@V2CTx, a finding directly attributed to the elevated total DOS near the Fermi level in V2CTx composites that enhances electron cloud distribution and electroconductivity20. Beyond these intrinsic electronic advantages, vanadium oxides have been independently shown to improve the OER activity of transition metal oxide composites through optimization of M–OH bond strength, suggesting that partial oxidation of the V2CTx scaffold during electrolysis may even contribute beneficially rather than detrimentally to overall catalytic performance. Furthermore, Schmiedecke et al. demonstrated that intentionally oxidized, partially exfoliated V2CTx enhanced the OER activity of CuCo composites compared to fresh V2CTx—a behavior entirely distinct from Ti3C2Tx, where oxidation irreversibly degrades conductivity and support functionality. This tolerance for oxidation is particularly relevant for practical electrolysis conditions, where anodic potentials and elevated temperatures inevitably drive surface restructuring of the catalyst support. Furthermore, V2CTx has been shown to form stronger metal-support interactions with transition metal catalysts compared to its titanium carbide counterpart, as reflected in the significant metal-support coupling reported in CuCo@V2CTx, which achieved an OER overpotential of 285 mV at 10 mA cm−2 while a comparable CuCo2O4@Ti3C2Tx reference showed substantially inferior performance 15. In our own previous works, we demonstrated that CoFe and NiFe based catalysts supported on V2CTx MXene-derived materials showed enhanced OER performance in AEM electrolyzers21,22. Building upon these findings, the presented study introduces a modified synthesis approach employing hydrothermal methods with ammonium fluoride (NH4F) as an additive. This synthetic strategy offers potential advantages such as improved control over particle size and morphology, enhanced interaction between the catalyst and support, and better dispersion of active sites. Herein, we report the systematic synthesis and characterization of CoFe@V2CTx composites with varying vanadium content (5–50 mol% V relative to Co + Fe). Through comprehensive structural, compositional, and electrochemical analysis, combined with advanced in-situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), we elucidate the structure-performance relationships and provide mechanistic insights into the enhanced OER activity. X-ray diffraction analysis was performed to investigate the crystalline structure and phase composition of the synthesized materials (Fig. 1b). The pure V2CTx MXene exhibited a sharp reflection at 7.3° corresponding to the (002) plane, which is characteristic of the c-axis stacking of MXene layers. Additionally, a broad peak with an underlying sharp peak at 14.5° corresponding to the (004) and a minor peak at 22.0° corresponding to the (006) plane were observed. The sharp (002) peak indicated well-defined interlayer spacing in the multilayer MXene structure, while the coexistence of sharp and broad features suggested a mixture of well-ordered and less-ordered stacking sequences within the material. The pure CoFe catalyst displayed two prominent reflections at 18.5° and 20.9°. The dominant peak at 18.5° (d = 4.84 Å) was assigned to the (111) reflection of a nanocrystalline cobalt-doped iron spinel phase (Co0.05Fe2.95O4, PDF 01-090-3646), a well-established product of Co2+/Fe3+ co-precipitation under hydrothermal conditions23,24,25,26. The secondary reflection at 20.9° was assigned to cobalt fluoride hydroxide (CoF1.3(OH)0.7, PDF 00-018-0405), which is consistent with the NH4F additive in the synthesis, providing a fluoride source for its formation. The broad minor reflections in the 32–36° region arise from the secondary peaks of CoF1.3(OH)0.7 in this angular range. The overall broad peak widths confirmed the predominantly nanocrystalline character of the pure CoFe material, consistent with the role of NH4F as a nucleation-controlling agent that promotes numerous small nuclei rather than fewer large crystals 27,28. Upon incorporation of V2CTx, significant systematic changes in the diffraction patterns were observed. Note that all CFV composition labels denote nominal V:(Co + Fe + V) molar ratios; measured values from ICP-OES deviate increasingly at higher V content, as discussed in the ICP-OES analysis (Fig. 4.) For low V content samples (CFV5 and CFV10), the spinel (111) reflection at 18.5° and the CoF1.3(OH)0.7 peak at 20.9° remained prominent, indicating that both solution-crystallized phases persisted as the dominant components. With increasing V2CTx content toward CFV17, the spinel and CoF1.3(OH)0.7 reflections diminished substantially, and a distinct new set of reflections appeared, reaching maximum intensity at CFV17 before declining in CFV33 and CFV50. The CFV17 pattern is dominated by two overlapping phase contributions that together account for all observed reflections. The peak cluster at approximately 12.0°, 17.0°, 27.0°, 35.2°, 46.6°, and 56.5° was assigned to tetragonal FeOOH (PDF 04-009-0709), which can be attributed to a CoFe-derived oxyhydroxide phase whose formation is templated by the V2CTx. The four most prominent reflections unique to CFV17 at approximately 52.9°, 39.7°, 34.4°, and 61.6° were assigned to cobalt fluoride hydroxide (CoFOH, PDF 00-018-0406). The 20.9° reflection, assigned to CoF1.3(OH)0.7 (PDF 00-018-0405) in pure CoFe, persisted across the CFV series, indicating that this solution-derived cobalt fluoride-hydroxide phase coexists with the interfacially nucleated CoFOH phase throughout the series. The selective crystallization of CoFOH specifically at CFV17 loading, rather than at lower or higher V2CTx content, is proposed to arise from a heterogeneous nucleation threshold. At low MXene loadings (CFV5, CFV10), the available V2CTx surface area is insufficient to redirect a significant fraction of CoFe nucleation away from solution-phase pathways, which yields CoF1.3(OH)0.7 and cobalt-iron spinel as the dominant crystalline products. As V2CTx loading increases toward CFV17, Co2+ ions preferentially adsorb at V–OH and V–O surface terminations. These terminations, combined with the surface-bound F from V2CTx etching, provide both the hydroxide and fluoride ligands required to nucleate the CoFOH phase directly at the MXene interface. Above CFV17, the Co2+/Fe3+ supply is distributed across a greater number of nucleation sites, resulting in progressive crystallographic disorder, evidenced by the near-disappearance of CFV33 and CFV50. Furthermore, in CFV33 and CFV50, the sharp V2CTx reflections at 7.3°, 14.5°, and 22.0° dominated the patterns, confirming that the MXene structural integrity was preserved. The CoFOH reflections diminished substantially, and the CoF1.3(OH)0.7 and spinel peaks progressively weakened, consistent with the dilution of CoFe phase content and the increasing MXene surface coverage observed by SEM. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was employed to examine the morphological features and structural evolution of the catalysts as a function of V2CTx content (Fig. 1c and Fig. S1). The cross-section of pure V2CTx MXene displayed characteristic vertically stacked layered sheets, typical of multilayer MXene structures. The pure CoFe catalyst exhibited a distinctly heterogeneous morphology, consisting of two coexisting structural features: relatively large octahedral crystals with dimensions of approximately 1 µm, and substantially smaller spherical nanoparticles with diameters of only a few nanometers. The octahedral crystals likely correspond to the spinel and cobalt fluoride-hydroxide phases identified in the XRD analysis (peaks at 18.45° and 20.9°), while the spherical nanoparticles represent even smaller or more amorphous CoFe species. Notably, the spherical nanoparticles in pure CoFe showed significant aggregation, forming dense clusters that may limit the accessibility of active sites. a Schematic of the three-step synthesis procedure: (1) HF/HCl etching, (2) TMAOH delamination, (3) hydrothermal hybridization. b Powder XRD patterns with reference PDF cards and c Scanning electron micrographs of V2CTx, CoFe, and CFV17 samples. Upon incorporation of V2CTx, the large octahedral crystals presented in pure CoFe disappeared in all CFV composites, starting at the lowest V2CTx loading (CFV5). This suppression of octahedral crystal formation upon V2CTx addition supports the XRD observations, where the characteristic peaks at 18.45° and 20.9° diminished with increasing V2CTx content. Instead, all CFV composites predominantly featured spherical nanoparticles uniformly distributed on the surface of flake-like MXene structures. The particle size of a few nm remained consistent across all CFV compositions, indicating that V2CTx content did not significantly affect the nucleation and growth of the nanoparticles themselves. Importantly, the spherical nanoparticles in the CFV composites appeared to be anchored onto the MXene sheets rather than simply physically mixed, suggesting strong interfacial interactions between the CoFe species and the V2CTx support. This anchoring effect was consistent with the absence of significant nanoparticle aggregation in the composites, contrasting sharply with the clustering observed in pure CoFe. The improved dispersion in CFV materials likely contributes to enhanced catalyst utilization and increased accessibility of active sites. Additionally, evidence of MXene degradation is observed in the form of delaminated sheet fragments, which may be attributed to the etching abilities of NH4F during hydrothermal synthesis. This partial exfoliation could potentially increase the specific surface area of the support and create additional anchoring sites for the CoFe nanoparticles. With increasing V2CTx content, the surface coverage of the MXene sheets by CoFe nanoparticles progressively decreased, i.e., more MXene surface was exposed. While at low V content (CFV5 and CFV10), the MXene sheets were densely decorated with nanoparticles in CFV50, substantial areas of bare MXene sheets were visible. This decreasing coverage correlated with the reduced CoFe: V2CTx ratio and may contribute to the diminished OER activity observed for CFV50, as fewer catalytically active CoFe sites are available per unit mass. The SEM observations thus provided morphological support for the volcano-shaped activity trend: CFV17 appears to achieve an optimal balance between sufficient CoFe nanoparticle loading for catalytic activity, good dispersion on the conductive V2CTx support, and the absence of detrimental large crystal formation, all of which contribute to its superior OER performance. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Fig. 2a) was employed to investigate the nanoscale morphology and interfacial structure of the pure materials and composites. TEM imaging confirmed the morphological trends observed by SEM, with CFV5 showing near-complete MXene coating and CFV50 sparse coverage. a Bright-field TEM, b HRTEM, c SAED patterns, and d ADF-STEM with corresponding EELS mapping. Moreover, high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) analysis revealed distinct crystallographic features across the sample series (Fig. 2b). The V2CTx (100) plane with a d-spacing of 0.27 nm was clearly resolved in both pure V2CTx and all CFV composites, confirming that the MXene integrity was preserved throughout the hydrothermal synthesis process. In pure CoFe, lattice fringes with a d-spacing of approximately 0.48 nm were observed, consistent with the (111) reflection of the cobalt-iron spinel phase (d = 4.84 Å, 2θ = 18.32°) identified as the dominant XRD phase in pure CoFe. Fringes at approximately 0.25 nm were also observed across all samples. This d-spacing fall was attributed to the CoF1.3(OH)0.7 reflection at 35.77° (d = 2.51 Å) identified by XRD. The CFV composites exhibited additional lattice spacings beyond those observed in pure CoFe. The 0.48 nm spacing persisted in CFV5-CFV17, reflecting the continued presence of the cobalt-iron spinel phase at these loadings, consistent with the weak-to-moderate spinel (111) peak retained in the XRD patterns of these samples. The appearance of a 0.74–0.75 nm spacing in CFV composites is particularly significant: this spacing is consistent with the (001) reflection of tetragonal FeOOH (PDF 04-009-0709, d = 7.38 Å at 11.98°), whose formation is promoted at the V2CTx interface as discussed in the XRD analysis. This fringe was absent in pure CoFe but emerged from the lowest V2CTx loading (CFV5), indicating that even limited MXene surface area is sufficient to initiate interfacial FeOOH nucleation, suggesting preferential Fe3+ adsorption at V–OH and V–O surface terminations. Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns provided critical insights into the crystalline structure evolution across the composite series (Fig. 2c). Pure CoFe displayed only diffuse rings at d≈2.5 Å without discrete diffraction spots, confirming its predominantly amorphous or nanocrystalline character consistent with the broad XRD reflections. The diffuse ring at d≈2.5 Å was consistent with the CoF1.3(OH)0.7 reflections in the 34–36° region. In contrast, the CFV composites exhibited discrete diffraction spots, indicating that V2CTx promoted the formation of more ordered crystalline phases. A spacing of approximately 0.74–0.75 nm appeared from CFV5, directly corresponding to the incipient tetragonal FeOOH (001) reflection (d = 7.38 Å) identified by XRD at 11.98°. The coexistence of smaller spacings (0.25–0.27 nm) indicated that the CoFe spinel and Co fluoride-hydroxide phases persisted alongside the interfacially nucleated FeOOH structure from the smallest MXene loadings. At the optimal loading (CFV17), the HRTEM image and SAED pattern became more complex, showing both the 0.74 nm spacing of tetragonal FeOOH (001) and smaller spacings of approximately 0.25–0.29 nm attributable to the CoFOH at 34.63° (d = 2.59 Å), and CoF1.3(OH)0.7 at 35.77° (d = 2.51 Å). The multiple discrete diffraction spots at different angles in CFV17 reflected the higher degree of crystallographic ordering relative to pure CoFe, consistent with V2CTx-templated interfacial nucleation of both FeOOH and CoFOH phases reaching their maximum abundance at this composition. At higher loadings (CFV33), a spacing of 0.60 nm was detected in SAED, consistent with the V2CTx (004) reflection at 14.5° (d = 6.1 Å). The loss of the 0.74 nm FeOOH spacing and the emergence of dominant V2CTx reflections suggested that the MXene support structurally predominated, and CoFe phase boundaries became increasingly blurred due to extensive Co/Fe/V intermixing. At the highest MXene loading (CFV50), only the V2CTx (100) plane remained visible in SAED, with complete absence of discrete CoFe phase reflections, confirming the XRD observation of the loss of CoFe crystallinity concomitant with the formation of disordered Co–Fe–V phases. Lattice fringe termination behavior corroborated the SAED structural evolution: abrupt fringe terminations at low loading (CFV5, CFV10) indicated preserved distinct CoFe crystallinity with sharp phase boundaries, while gradual transitions at higher loadings reflected progressive atomic-scale integration of Co, Fe, and V. Annular dark-field scanning TEM (ADF-STEM) imaging coupled with EELS elemental mapping revealed the spatial distribution of Co, Fe, V, and F across the samples (Fig. 2d). Pure V2CTx showed V signals predominantly, while pure CoFe exhibited homogeneous Co/Fe mixing without V. In the CFV composites, Co and Fe signals were strongly co-localized at visible CoFe particles anchored on the MXene sheets. Fluorine signals were detected universally across all samples, arising from F present both in the V2CTx surface terminations (from HF etching) and in the fluoride-hydroxide phases (CoFOH, CoF1.3(OH)0.7) formed during NH4F-mediated hydrothermal synthesis. Critically, even regions of apparently uncovered MXene exhibited detectable Co and Fe signals, indicating atomic-scale dispersion or sub-monolayer coverage beyond the resolution of conventional TEM imaging. The elemental maps revealed increasing Co/Fe/V intermixing from CFV5 to CFV50, correlating with the progressive loss of CoFe crystallinity observed by both XRD and SAED. High V2CTx content in CFV33 and CFV50 inhibited discrete particle nucleation, instead promoting the formation of intermixed Co–Fe–V phases with diffuse boundaries. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy was performed on pure V2CTx, CoFe, and composites CFV5-CFV50 to probe surface oxidation states and electronic interactions across the loading series (Fig. 3, Fig. S2). As all XPS spectra with the exception of pure V2CTx were charge-corrected by referencing the C 1s C─C peak of the carbon tape substrate to 285.0 eV, reported binding energies carry a systematic offset of +0.2 eV relative to the conventional adventitious carbon reference of 284.8 eV. One exception is pure V2CTx, which exhibited no measurable charging owing to its metallic conductivity and required no charge correction. Consequently, the C–C peak of pure V2CTx appears at its true binding energy of ~284.2 eV, consistent with sp2/sp3 graphitic carbon in the MXene lattice. The apparent ~0.8 eV C–C peak offset between pure V2CTx and the composite samples, therefore, reflects the difference between uncorrected and charge-corrected spectra, not a chemical or electronic change in the carbon environment. As the composite powder samples retained residual charging effects despite correction, the reported absolute binding energies should be interpreted with caution; trends across the sample series are considered more reliable than absolute values. The convergence of structural and spectroscopic evidence identifies interfacial V–O–Fe coordination as the central mechanistic principle governing OER enhancement in CFV composites. XRD identified tetragonal FeOOH as an interfacially nucleated phase in CFV17, whose formation at the V2CTx surface necessitates oxygen-bridged Fe3+ coordination with the V–OH and V–O surface terminations of the MXene. STXM confirmed that both V and Fe are more oxidized in the composites relative to their isolated counterparts, while Co remains invariant, consistent with V–O–Fe bridging at the FeOOH/V2CTx heterointerface, withdrawing electron density from both metal centers through the shared oxygen. Operando XANES revealed that in CFV17, the transition to high-valent Co species occurred ~150 mV earlier than in pure CoFe, while simultaneously, the Fe K-edge in CFV17 advanced to energies not reached in pure CoFe under operating potentials. The earlier and more complete oxidation of both active metals in CFV17 directly explains its lower overpotential, as high-valent Co3+ and Fe3+/Fe4+ species are widely recognized as the active sites for OER in alkaline media. EXAFS analysis further showed that V2CTx stabilized the Co–O bond distance and prevented the Fe coordination shell collapse observed in pure CoFe under prolonged polarization, providing a structural basis for the superior durability of CFV17. The volcano-shaped activity profile across the CFV series thus reflects a competition between two opposing effects: electronic activation of the CoFe phase through V–O–Fe interfacial coupling, which strengthens with increasing V2CTx content, and active site accessibility, which deteriorates as MXene surface coverage rises above CFV17. Below CFV17, the V–Fe coupling is underdeveloped, and the activation benefit is not fully realized. Above CFV17, surface CoFe coverage drops and charge transfer resistance rises as inactive V2CTx shields the CoFe/electrolyte interface. An additional contribution to the self-activation at CFV17 arises from the CoFOH phase identified by XRD, which reaches its maximum crystalline abundance at this composition and tracks the OER activity volcano across the series. Under alkaline OER conditions, CoFOH is expected to convert progressively to Co oxyhydroxide with concurrent release of F−, generating defect-rich active Co sites during the initial stages of operation—consistent with the transient performance evolution observed in chronopotentiometry. CFV17 thus occupies the unique compositional space where interfacial electronic activation is maximally developed, active site density is preserved, and the CoFOH-mediated fluoride activation is at its peak, collectively yielding the lowest overpotential at 10 mA cm−2 and sustained performance over 24 h at 100 mA cm−2. This study demonstrated that hydrothermal synthesis using NH4F enabled the fabrication of highly active CoFe@V2CTx MXene composite catalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction. Through systematic variation of the vanadium content, an optimal composition was identified, CFV17 (17 mol% V), that exhibited a reduced overpotential of 304 ± 6.6 mV at 10 mA cm−2, an improvement over pure CoFe catalysts, and the lowest Tafel slope in the series (39.3 ± 2.7 mV dec−1), indicating the most facile OER kinetics. EIS confirmed a 2.5-fold reduction in charge transfer resistance relative to pure CoFe. Comprehensive characterization provided detailed insight into the structural and electronic origins of this performance. XRD revealed that V2CTx suppressed the formation of catalytically inert octahedral crystals present in pure CoFe and promoted the interfacial nucleation of tetragonal FeOOH and CoFOH. Bulk electronic structure characterization by STXM revealed simultaneous oxidation of V and Fe in the as-synthesized composites, with Co remaining in the Co2+ resting state across the series. This is consistent with V–O–Fe bridging coordination at the FeOOH/V2CTx heterointerface, where the interfacially nucleated FeOOH phase structurally necessitates oxygen-mediated contact between Fe3+ and V–OH/V–O surface terminations. This interfacial electronic coupling is proposed to lower the energetic barrier for electrochemical generation of OER-active high-valent species under applied potential. Operando XAS confirmed that CFV17 achieved the formation of high-valent Co and Fe species approximately 150 mV earlier than pure CoFe. EXAFS analysis further revealed that V2CTx prevented the Fe coordination shell collapse observed in pure CoFe during prolonged OER, stabilizing the active metal sites structurally. The volcano-shaped activity trend was rationalized as a competition between increasing electronic activation of the CoFe phase through V–O–Fe interfacial coupling with increasing V2CTx content, and active site dilution, which becomes detrimental above CFV17. An additional contribution arises from the CoFOH phase, which reaches maximum abundance at CFV17 and is proposed to generate defect-rich active Co sites through conversion to Co oxyhydroxide under alkaline OER conditions. CFV17 uniquely occupied the composition space where interfacial electronic activation, active site accessibility, and CoFOH-mediated site generation were optimally balanced. These findings establish a rational design principle for MXene-supported electrocatalysts: engineering metal-support interfacial bonding to activate the CoFe phase electronically while preserving sufficient active phase surface exposure and leveraging fluoride-hydroxide phase transformations as an additional source of active site generation. The synthesis of V2CTx MXenes was carried out through chemical etching utilizing a mixture of hydrofluoric (HF, 48%, Sigma-Aldrich) acid and hydrochloric acid (HCl, 37%, Sigma-Aldrich) for 72 h at 50 °C. Initially, 16 ml of HCl was added to 24 ml of HF at room temperature and stirred in a polypropylene reaction flask. Afterward, 2 g of the precursor V2AlC (40 μm, Carbon Ukraine) was added stepwise to avoid overheating. Following the etching process, 130 ml of ultra pure water was mixed to the resulting black acid suspension in a 150 ml Falcon tube and centrifuged three times at 3500 rpm for 5 min each in order to remove any residual acid. Multilayered V2C obtained after the last centrifugation cycle was, first, intercalated with 40 mL of 5 wt% tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAOH, 25% w/w, Thermo Scientific) at room temperature under stirring for 6 h. The black basic solution was washed with water, followed by two centrifugation cycles at 3500 rpm for 10 min. Lastly, for the collection of delaminated V2CTx, the sediment was diluted and washed at 2500 rpm for 10 min and shaken for at least 2 min to ensure the sediment dispersion. The step was repeated until the disappearance of delaminated MXenes in the supernatant. The suspended MXenes were concentrated through centrifugation at 8000 rpm for 5 min and the concentration was measured by vacuum filtering 1 ml of the final V2CTx suspension. CoFe@V2CTx composites with varying vanadium content were synthesized via a one-pot hydrothermal method. In a typical synthesis, cobalt(II) nitrate hexahydrate (Co(NO3)2·6H2O, 116.41 mg, 0.4 mmol, 99.99%, Sigma-Aldrich), iron(III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, 80.80 mg, 0.2 mmol, 99.99%, Sigma-Aldrich), urea (CO(NH2)2, 180.18 mg, 3 mmol, 99.0–100.5%, Sigma-Aldrich), and ammonium fluoride (NH4F, 44.45 mg, 1.2 mmol, 99%, Sigma-Aldrich) were dissolved in ultrapure water under sonication until complete dissolution was achieved. To prepare composites with different V:(Co + Fe) molar ratios, appropriate volumes of V2CTx aqueous dispersion were added to achieve nominal 5, 10, 17, 33, and 50 mol% V relative to the total metal content (V + Co + Fe). The specific masses of V2CTx (assuming V2CF2 composition with molecular weight of 151.89 g/mol) required for each composition were: CFV5 (2.40 mg), CFV10 (5.06 mg), CFV17 (9.33 mg), CFV33 (22.44 mg), and CFV50 (45.57 mg). The mixture was then diluted to a total aqueous volume of 5 ml with ultrapure water, followed by the addition of N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, 2.5 ml, Sigma-Aldrich) and dimethyl phthalate (DMP, 2.5 ml, Sigma-Aldrich) as co-solvents. The resulting mixture was transferred to a polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)-lined stainless steel autoclave. The sealed autoclave was heated in an oven at 100 °C for 12 h and then allowed to cool naturally to room temperature. The precipitate was collected by centrifugation and washed three times with ultrapure water and once with ethanol to remove residual salts and organic solvents. The final product was dried overnight under vacuum at room temperature. For comparison, a pure CoFe catalyst (without V2CTx) was synthesized following the identical procedure described above, omitting only the addition of V2CTx dispersion. Elemental composition analysis was carried out using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) on an iCAP 7400 Duo Full MFC instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated in axial mode. Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were conducted on a Bruker D8 ADVANCE diffractometer equipped with a Cu Kα radiation source (λ1 = 0.1541 nm, λ2 = 0.1544 nm). Diffractograms were acquired over an angular range of 5° to 110° (2θ) with a step size of 0.0131° and a dwell time of 1.25 s per step. Morphological examination was performed using a Zeiss MERLIN field emission gun scanning electron microscope (FEG-SEM) operating at 0.1 to 30 keV. Samples for SEM analysis were mounted on aluminum specimen holders using adhesive carbon tape. Micrographs were captured at 1.0 kV electron high tension (EHT) with a 40 mA probe current using a secondary electron (SE2) detector. XPS measurements were conducted using a JEOL JPS-9030 setup with a base pressure of 2 ∙ 10−9 mbar. The powders were evenly distributed on carbon tape for the measurements. A non-monochromated Mg source with 300 W power was used for excitation. A hemispherical analyzer with a pass energy of 50 eV (surveys) and 20 eV (narrow scans) was used to detect the emitted photoelectrons, yielding a resolution of 1.0 eV. The binding energy scale of the analyzer was calibrated by setting the Au 4f7/2 and the Cu 2p3/2 peaks of clean gold and copper foils to 84.00 and 932.67 eV, respectively. However, since all the samples (except for pure V2C) showed charging, the binding energy of the C─C peak of the carbon tape was shifted to 285.0 eV for comparison. Sensitivity factors were calculated using the experimentally determined transmission function of the analyzer, the atomic cross sections after Scofield42, and the inelastic mean free path for elements given by Seah and Dench43. Peak fitting was performed using CasaXPS44. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and annular dark-field scanning TEM (ADF-STEM) were performed using an uncorrected FEI Titan with Schottky field emission S-FEG source operated at 300 kV. Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) mapping was carried out with a Quantum Gatan Imaging Filter (GIF) detector with energy dispersion of 0.5 eV per channel. Scanning transmission X-ray microscopy (STXM) measurements were performed at the MAXYMUS endstation (UE-46 beamline, BESSY II, HZB). Absorption spectra at the V L-edge (510–535 eV), Co L-edge (770–800 eV), and Fe L-edge (700–735 eV) were acquired by scanning the focused X-ray beam across the sample and detecting transmitted flux with an avalanche photodiode. Optical density spectra were calculated as OD = −ln(I/I0), where I0 is the incident intensity measured on clean membrane regions. Powder samples (V2CTx, CoFe, CFV17, CFV33) were dispersed in water/isopropanol at 10 mg mL−1 with 8 µL Nafion as a binder. Following 10 min ultrasonication, inks were diluted 1:250 (4 µL ink in 1 mL solvent) and deposited as 4 µL droplets onto 100 nm thick silicon nitride membranes (1 × 1 mm2 window area, Silson) supported by 5 × 5 mm2 Si frames. Samples were dried at room temperature, and measurement areas were identified by optical microscopy prior to loading onto the STXM holder. Two spectroscopic metrics were extracted from V L-edge data: (1) the L3/L2 branching ratio, calculated from peak intensities at ~518 eV and ~525 eV, which tracks vanadium oxidation state through d-electron count; and (2) the t2g/eg intensity ratio within the L3 manifold (~517 eV and ~518 eV features), which reflects octahedral crystal field splitting and V–O covalency. Peak positions were identified from spectral line shapes, and intensity ratios were computed directly from optical density values. Operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) experiments were carried out at the SAMBA beamline of the SOLEIL synchrotron facility, Paris-Saclay. Catalyst dispersions were drop-cast onto flexible graphite foil substrates to form working electrodes, which were subsequently dried at 60 °C on a hot plate. The XAS measurements utilized a purpose-built three-electrode electrochemical cell comprising the prepared working electrode, a platinum wire counter electrode, and a Hg/HgO reference electrode. Fluorescence mode XAS spectra were acquired at the Co and Fe K-edges with the detector positioned at 45° to the working electrode surface. Energy calibration was achieved using Co, Fe, and V metal foils as reference standards. The measurement protocol began with ex situ XAS characterization of the catalysts and reference materials. Following this, the electrochemical cell was filled with N2-saturated 1 M NaOH electrolyte, and spectra were recorded at open circuit potential (OCP). Operando measurements were then conducted under chronoamperometric conditions at applied potentials of 0.93, 1.23, 1.38, 1.53, and 1.68 V versus Hg/HgO, with XAS data collected at each potential step. After completion of the potential sequence, a final spectrum was acquired at OCP. Metal oxide references were prepared in the same procedure as the catalysts, but were measured ex situ, i.e., in the same cell but without the addition of NaOH. XAS data processing and analysis were performed using Fastosh software (v1.0.9)45. Edge positions in the X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) region were determined via the half-edge step method. The normalized absorption spectra were converted to k-space and weighted by k2. Fourier transformation was carried out over a k-range of 1.5–10 Å−1 using a Hanning window function, yielding radial distribution functions displayed over an R-range of 0–6 Å. Catalyst inks were prepared by dispersing 10 mg of each catalyst material in a mixture containing 496 µl of deionized water, 496 µl of isopropanol, and 8 µl of Nafion solution. This ink dispersion (1.13 µl) was then drop-cast onto a glassy carbon rotating disk electrode (RDE) with a geometric area of 0.0707 cm2, which had been polished with 0.05 µm alumina prior to use. The electrode was dried under a gentle nitrogen flow, yielding a catalyst loading of 0.16 mg cm−2. Electrochemical measurements were performed using a CHI760E potentiostat in a standard three-electrode configuration. The setup consisted of the catalyst-coated glassy carbon RDE as the working electrode, a Hg/HgO electrode as the reference, and a carbon rod as the counter electrode. All experiments were conducted in N2-saturated 1 M NaOH electrolyte prepared from deionized water (18.2 MΩ cm resistivity, Barnstead Smart2Pure Pro Water Purification System, Thermo Scientific). The working electrode was rotated at 1600 rpm throughout all RDE measurements unless specified otherwise. Prior to each set of measurements, electrodes were conditioned via chronopotentiometry at 10 mA cm−2 for 60 s or until potential stabilization. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves were recorded at a scan rate of 1 mV/s with automatic iR compensation applied by the potentiostat. Potentials measured versus Hg/HgO were converted to overpotential (η) using the equation η = Eappl + E0(Hg/HgO) + 0.059 pH − E0(H2O/O2), where E0(Hg/HgO) = 0.098 V at 25 °C and E0(H2O/O2) = 1.23 V. The overpotential at 10 mA cm−2 (η10) was determined from the iR-corrected LSV curves, and mean values were calculated from at least three independent electrode preparations per material, with standard deviations reported as error bars. Tafel slopes were extracted from the linear portion of the Tafel plots derived from the LSV data. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted using two approaches: (1) galvanostatic EIS at 10 mA cm−2 over a frequency range of 0.1–100,000 Hz to determine charge transfer resistance (Rct) during OER, and (2) potentiostatic EIS at applied potentials of 1.50, 1.55, 1.60, and 1.65 V versus RHE across the same frequency range. Nyquist plots were corrected for the series resistance (Rs) specific to each electrode. Electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) was determined from the double-layer capacitance (Cdl) measured via cyclic voltammetry. Multiple CVs were performed over a 100 mV potential window in a non-Faradaic region at scan rates ranging from 1 to 100 mV/s. The anodic and cathodic capacitive currents recorded with a stationary working electrode were plotted against the scan rate, and Cdl was obtained by averaging the absolute values of the anodic and cathodic slopes. ECSA was calculated by dividing Cdl by the specific capacitance of transition metals in 1 M NaOH (CF = 0.04 mF cm−2). Cyclic voltammetry was performed at a scan rate of 40 mV/s for electrochemical characterization. For electrocatalytic stability tests, chronopotentiometry was conducted at a constant current of 100 mA cm−2 for 24 h. As WE, a 1.0 cm2 nickel fiber felt (35 μm fiber diameter, 0.5 mm thickness, 80% porosity, Xinxiang Aida Machinery Equipment Corporation, China) was used. Nickel fiber felts were cleaned by sonicating in 20% HCl for 20 min followed by sonicating subsequently in DI water, acetone, isopropanol, ethanol, and DI water for 10 min each, before being coated with 1.0 mg of catalytic material. The datasets generated and/or analyzed during the current study are not publicly available due to their large size and the computational resources required for storage, but are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. title: This KFC Meal Unlocks an Exclusive BTS V Collectible | Outlook Respawn - Outlook Respawn
content: The exclusive BTS V accordion postcard is available at KFC Malaysia alongside a new K-series menu. Fast-food giant KFC Malaysia has launched a K-series menu, which comes along with collectibles. At the center of this menu are the seaweed-seasoned wrap and shaker fries, which unlock access to an exclusive, add-on accordion postcard featuring BTS member V, also known as Kim Taehyung. According to reports from The Smart Local Malaysia, the collectibles will be available from June 4 through July 6, 2026, nationwide, but only as an upsell with the combo meal order. The postcard costs an additional RM17.10 (~ $4.24 USD) and features five photos of V as well as his signature. The photos showcase the BTS star as Coca-Cola Zero's ambassador, highlighting a calculated cross-brand partnership. Reportedly, V’s Coca-Cola endorsements are rapidly expanding across Asian markets. In Hong Kong, similar types of postcards, stickers, and accordion photobooks were available through certain kinds of beverage and meal purchases. The campaign arrives at a time of surging BTS regional momentum, as the group is set to begin its Asia leg of the ARIRANG world tour in the latter half of the year. Therefore, to leverage on this massive consumer urgency, major global businesses across Asia are moving swiftly to capitalize on the momentum. Although The Smart Local Malaysia has reported on the campaign, KFC Malaysia has yet to issue a statement regarding the same. Details of exact stock allocations, individual purchase limits, or potential outlet exclusions are not yet confirmed by the relevant authorities. Nevertheless, for the local fanbase of BTS or V, in particular, this does little to deter the demand and converts a routine multi-market retail rollout into a competitive, localized hunt for a piece of pop history. title: Majority of Measure V votes oppose Davis housing project as the race tightens - Abridged – PBS KVIE
content: The measure will decide the fate of the Village Farms housing development The latest drop of election results continues to show a tight Measure V race, with “no” slightly outpacing “yes.” With more ballots left to count, the “no” campaign had slightly more than 51% of the vote as of about late Friday afternoon, while “yes” had a little more than 48%. To move ahead, the project would need a simple majority of Davis voters to approve it. If the “yes” campaign reaches that threshold, the Village Farms development is cleared to move forward with up to 1,800 residential units just west of the Wildhorse neighborhood. The construction timeline hasn’t been finalized, but it would likely take years to complete. If voters reject the project, it will die in its current form. Should the landowners decide to propose a new development, they would need to go through the entire approval process again. Village Farms was first proposed in 2023. While results show a majority of votes opposing the measure, the election will not be certified until all votes are counted, and it’s still a close race. The county will continue to share updates with the next batch of results expected Tuesday. No on V, spearheaded by Eileen Samitz, raised concerns about the environmental consequences of the project, its proximity to the old Davis landfill, traffic and what the campaign says is an inadequate affordable housing plan. Yes on V was funded by the North Davis Land Co., which was established by the group of developers behind the project, including John Whitcombe. The campaign touted the project’s potential to increase Davis’ struggling housing stock and sagging school enrollment rates. In addition to housing, the proposal includes a list of baseline project features and an affordable housing plan. Daniel Hennessy joins Abridged from the California Local News Fellowship. title: Maserati MCPura Cielo vs. McLaren Artura Spider: Which Convertible V-6 Supercar Takes the Win? - Road & Track
content: Tops down, engines ringing to the redline, and an empty California canyon road to play on—it rarely gets better than this. Electrification is arriving at almost every level of the auto industry, including the very top. The Maserati MCPura is one of the most beautiful supercars of this era, but it's also one of the last ones that doesn't have to carry the weight of a high-voltage battery or the additional complexity of an electric motor. Instead, there's a ripping twin-turbo V-6 engine, power to the rear wheels, and an old-school elegance where form and function meld in a stylish fusion, especially in the open-topped Cielo version you see here. Could this be peak analog supercar? The McLaren Artura Spider takes the other, more modern path, integrating a high-tech and highly potent hybrid powertrain with design that plays on many of the themes familiar from McLarens over the last 15 years. Despite the very different approaches, the prices for both are very similar. So let's get to the very serious business of determining which deserves garage privileges when your ship comes in. It doesn't get any more straightforward than this when it comes to roofless Italian supercars in 2026. Maserati fits its power-dense Nettuno 3.0-liter twin-turbo V-6 right behind the cabin. An eight-speed, paddle-shifted dual-clutch transmission transmits power through either a mechanical limited-slip diff, or as on our test car, an optional $2650 electronically controlled LSD. There's no hybrid system involved, just a whole lot of boost and Maserati's signature twin-spark-plug pre-chamber combustion tech. Peaks of 621 hp and 538 lb-ft of torque are enough for a claimed 2.9-second run to 60 mph. The only performance add-on our MCPura lacked was the $11,500 option of carbon-ceramic brakes. McLaren also chooses a 3.0-liter twin-turbo V-6 for the engine powering its junior supercar, but one with a electric motor to give a seriously potent electric boost. The combined power output sits at a Maserati-eclipsing 690 hp. Yet, surprisingly, despite the e-motor's contribution, the Artura has less peak torque at 531 lb-ft. Without the electrical side of the powertrain, the McLaren would be well short of Maserati, given that the small axial-flux motor that sits within the housing for the eight-speed dual-clutch transmission makes 94 hp and up to 166 lb-ft in its own right. The Artura even has a somewhat pokey EV mode, good for an EPA-rated 11 miles when the 7.4-kWh battery pack is fully charged. One other surprise is weight. Hybridization normally carries a chunky mass penalty, but when it comes to the quoted dry curb weight for each car, the Artura's 3212 pounds makes it over 300 pounds lighter than the 3565-pound pure-combustion Maserati. Lockwood Valley Road in Ventura County, California, is officially closed to through traffic. Flooding a couple of years ago washed out about 100 yards of pavement, but it's actually passable in dry conditions should you be adventurous enough to traverse the gap on a temporarily built dirt shoulder. The road itself is well worth the effort, with 26 miles of beautiful pavement to be experienced in peace. A few wide-open straights leave space to enjoy trips to the redline, while climbs up and down big hills and small mountains give the perfect opportunity to experience chassis balance on challenging corners and hairpins. The road logically passes through Lockwood Valley, an old borax mining area with views of Mount Pinos, the highest peak in Ventura County, in the distance. When the Maserati MC20 launched four years ago it was kind of a big deal. Maserati hadn't made a supercar since the MC12, the Ferrari Enzo–derived homologation special that was limited to just 50 examples. Now renamed, but otherwise barely touched, the MCPura stands alone in the world of Maseratis, as well as in today's hybrid-heavy world of supercars. While the McLaren adopts its typical dead-serious attitude of going about the business of going fast, the MCPura appeals more to the grand-touring-minded. The Maserati is a little softer than the McLaren in nearly every respect, but it still kicked ass when I wanted it to. The single best feature is easily the rowdy Nettuno V-6 powerplant. With the top down, the engine never stops talking, and while the turbos require some revs to come to the boil, I can't nominate a car that brings you along for the spooling process in a better auditory fashion than the MCPura. Letting off throttle was just as entertaining, air rushing back with a loud stu-tu-tu. A V-8 thrum would admittedly be nice, but I appreciate a theatrical V-6 nearly as much, and the MCPura's engine delivers endless charisma. The only thing it needs is a ridiculous exhaust, because this stock box fails to enthusiastically announce its riotous intentions to passersby. On the flip, the most alarming initial impression was the MCPura's brake pedal. It's spongy and entirely un-supercar-like around town. Past the initial bite point, the tuning starts to make sense with firmed-up responses, and it is also where the standard steel brakes offer greater feedback. I know from previous experience that the pedal is oddly wooden and devoid of feel with the carbon-ceramics, but the regular brakes felt progressive and naturally modulated once I had pushed past the initial spongy tip-in. Unfortunately, the steel brakes are also prone to fade. I experienced this a couple of times when trying to keep pace with the Artura. This was indicated first by the smell of hard-worked pads, then a lack of effectiveness and not a lengthening pedal. Also, to my surprise, the MCPura's front Michelin Pilot Sport 4S tires would heat up to the point of creating understeer at a similar rate. This was happening at pretty high speeds—it could be managed by compound upgrades or simply driving the car within its happy zone. When you're in that balanced place, the MCPura is downright joyous. Chassis engineers have nailed the braking balance into corners, making trailing the rear end and bending it to your will an instinctive, easy process. The rear end could be snappy when I got hard on the power before the rear tires had warmed up. But, once in a groove, I found I could trust the rear axle to deal with earlier and harder throttle applications. The MCPura's Sport and Corsa drive modes were best suited to California canyon roads. The Maserati's adaptive dampers never got too stiff or bouncy, hewing to that GT-like personality. The transmission's manual mode was essential for a road like Lockwood Valley, as the automatic shift programing doesn't hold gears or grab downshifts when slowing especially competently. Personally, I'm fine with being in charge, and the column-mounted, carbon-fiber paddles bring plenty-quick shifts from the dual-clutch, making it easy to keep the V-6 in the meat of its powerband. Considering how happy the MCPura is to be driven like a supercar, its best trick is simply how easy and sedate it is taking on normal tasks. The carbon-fiber monocoque is rigid and the cabin loud enough to mean its driver never forgets they are in an Italian supercar. But I felt I could take it on a four-plus-hour drive with very few complaints. I'd be a little more annoyed doing the same in the Artura. But what the McLaren gives up in refinement is worth it for what happens when you put your foot down. McLaren found itself in hot water during the initial Artura launch. From feedback that the new car wasn't hard core enough to some well-publicized reliability woes with the new hybrid powertrain, the brand's junior supercar caught plenty of critical flak. When the Spider came out two years later, McLaren took great care to address those concerns, with most of the same updates passed to the coupe at the same time. The end result is a car that, while still lacking the maniacal V-8 of the more expensive 750S, can proudly stand on its own. The McLaren's hybrid V-6 powertrain is nothing like the engine in the Maserati. The MCPura is peaky and requires effort to extract performance. The Artura Spider delivers speed effortlessly. Both engines see peak power hit at 7500 rpm, but the McLaren's sensation of torque from its hot-V turbo setup is pure buttery smoothness the whole way up there. The Maserati needs to be revved out, while the Artura can be short-shifted with seemingly little penalty. That electric motor fills in the deficits of the V-6, making the McLaren feel faster at practically every step. The Artura's quoted 0-to-60 time of 3.0 seconds is a tenth off Maserati's claim, but there isn't a single circumstance where the McLaren presents as slower. It is, after all, both lighter and more powerful than the MCPura. There's a certain instrumental purity to the McLaren V-6's sound as the revs rise upward to the engine's 8500-rpm redline, 500 rpm more than the Maserati's. Both the extra room in the tachometer and sound crescendo at the top of the range were appreciated over the MCPura, although the sensation of briefly banging against the Artura's rev limiter in auto transmission mode before the gearbox shifted up felt a little contrived in the context of this engineering marvel of a powertrain. I'd have the Maserati's engine for a casual blast through the mountains for its sound alone, but there's no denying McLaren has a big leg up when it comes to sheer performance and is only a quarter step behind in drama. McLaren makes up for that experiential deficit, and then some, the first time you turn the wheel. There's nothing all that objectionable about the MCPura's steering, but it can't compete with the electrohydraulic rack in the McLaren. With the wheel properly devoid of buttons, my hands had as direct a link to the Artura's front tires on the road as any modern performance car offers today. It's a part of the experience that never stopped being wonderful, from tootling through LA congestion to charging hard into a corner on a mountain road. The Maserati's steering is damn good among electric steering racks, but switching from it to the McLaren's is like slipping on a pair of 20/20-vision goggles and seeing the road in an entirely new light. Plus, as friendly as the MCPura Cielo is on any surface, the Artura Spider does it better with its Proactive Damping Control technology. I was only able to trip the car up in particularly bumpy braking zones, but its competence and forgiving nature was outstanding. Grip levels were higher than I remember from the old McLaren 570S, thanks to upgrades including wider front tires. I was confident to carry speed in long sweepers and trust the Pirelli P Zero rubber to stay glued. Add to that a brake pedal that felt perfectly connected in terms of both weight and feedback, and I found myself easily driving the Artura harder with greater ease than the Maserati. I suspect the advantage would widen considerably should a racetrack be involved, but even on road the difference was obvious. The McLaren's driver-focused characteristics are complemented by its spectacularly driver-focused interior. You sit lower than you do in the MCPura by a noticeable margin, but it's not any harder to slide in or out of the Artura's comfortable sport seats. Visibility forward and back is another huge boon of the Spider. The Maserati can feel a bit confining with larger A-pillars, whereas the cab-forward design of the McLaren made me feel like an integrated part of the car. Maserati totally wins when it comes to in-car tech, though. Most supercar makers force you to deal with their arcane and bespoke infotainment systems, but the MCPura simply uses the same UConnect 5 setup as any other Stellantis vehicle. It just works, and that's a huge stress reliever when you're piloting a quarter-million-plus-dollar car through a traffic catastrophe in LA. McLaren's system in the Artura is a nice upgrade over its previous software, but it still falls into the category of "weird and complicated supercar tech suite." The one big ease-of-life aspect McLaren nails that Maserati completely fails at is convertible roof operation. Maserati forces you to make a couple of clicks on the touchscreen before holding down on a small tile the whole time the roof is going up or down. Inevitably, you'll start the roof operation before Android Auto or Apple CarPlay has fully booted up, which automatically kicks you out of the top operation screen, causing the car to complain that the roof is partially closed and forcing another couple clicks back to the top operation command center. McLaren smartly just puts a switch in the dome-light area that requires no thought or attention to use, particularly helpful if you're trying to quickly get the top up while moving. Thankfully, both cars have roll-down rear center windows that allow engine and exhaust noise to filter directly into the cabin, even if you have the top up. There's nearly a whole C8 Corvette worth of options applied to this MCPura Cielo, and the largest chunk of that cost is the $21,510 AI Aqua Rainbow paint it's rocking from Maserati's Fuoriserie program. Also enormously expensive is the Maserati Trident in AI Aqua being placed on the tonneau for $11,390. This touch is a Fuoriserie option, as is the Fuoriserie logo in white ($1270) on the rear fender. Those 20-inch Cyclonic wheels in a diamond-cut finish cost $4000, and black-painted brake calipers are another $1380. The bright-blue theme continues inside with the Fuoriserie AI Aqua upholstery option that costs $8730. The heated seats are only $580, but the plenty nice-sounding Sonus Faber audio system is $4600. An interior carbon-fiber package totals $5300, while the ADAS package costs $4600. Lastly, the electronic limited-slip diff costs $2650. Plenty of money can be saved here by skipping the Fuoriserie bits, but I could never mount an argument against this paint. The Artura Spider has just under a Civic Type R's price in options. So in other words, its extras are quite modest when compared to the Maserati. The MSO Shibuya Spirit exterior paint is a reasonable $9800, and a Stealth Black exterior pack adds another $3300. Ten-spoke forged wheels cost $5100, and finishing them in black is another $1800. Its interior is full of black Alcantara as part of the Performance Theme that runs $9700. A Technology pack costs $7600, and the sport exhaust that you definitely want is $5300. These are two exceptional supercars that are markedly different from one another. I can wholeheartedly say that one or the other could be the better choice depending on what the use case is. Fancy dinners where curb appeal is king and the occasional canyon blast would suit the Maserati, while the Artura would cater to the more serious supercar buyer who might even consider tracking it. It also has the added bonus of being able to escape the neighborhood or cruise through city streets in total silence should you wish to move along under the radar. I would be grabbing the keys to the Artura Spider in almost every circumstance, making it the winner here. The MCPura is a brilliant car and the standout highlight in the current Maserati lineup. But, unfortunately for Maserati, the Artura does nearly all the daily-driver tasks just as well and feels a little bit better in almost every respect when exercised the way it’s meant to be. Both are true supercars. I walked away from my last hard drive in the Maserati exhausted but vibrating with energy. The McLaren left me shaking my head at just how capable it is, while not giving away an inch of integration between man and machine. It was one hell of a day at the office.
